title: Majestic Pawn
reviewNotes: All 35 board diagrams/captions reviewed; native image23 at 69 seconds confirms thirteen-piece root after Bg6. Complete finite mating proof checks all five defenses to Qc1+, including both knight blocks and both rook blocks, rather than assuming every sacrifice is accepted. Five teaching branches cover source double-queen/bishop sacrifice and representative independent blocks. Earlier promotion/trade/unique-move claims remain outside scope. Prior legal-only reconstruction is preserved.
transcript: fools will lose. Wise players will make a draw. But only a true genius would be able to win this incredible position. You see, white can get a new queen. But after black blocks the check. If we try to rush and trade this queen, actually we end in this end game where after picking up two pieces, we have queen against two pawns, rook and bishop. And white will be able to make a draw with best play and by being careful. But I can already tell you that any other move that is not promoting to the queen here will lose the game for white. So white has no choice but to get this new queen. But now after the black queen covers the check, white has to be a little bit more creative. So white plays queen to c6 check setting up a little trap. If black covers the check with the rook like this, actually this is a check between two moves after bishop to D2 using the pin on the black rook. The king moves and the pawn takes checkmate. But black is not that naive. Black plays bishop to G6. And now there are no tricks because if we play bishop to D2, the rook is simply going to take the bishop and white is going to lose. So it's pretty obvious that white has no followup and he should resign here, right? Well, not exactly. White is actually completely winning thanks to an incredible sequence starting with queen C1 check. A move that again prepares a checkmate in two moves. But of course this queen can just be taken for free by the rook. But white follows up with bishop D2 check. Another brilliant move. Again there is this checkmate threat except that the rook can simply take the bishop. And now you might wonder what even was the point of these sacrifices. What have we achieved? Well, you see this rook used to pin this white pawn and this rook used to attack the pawn from behind. We are trying to remove the pressure from this pawn. Why, you might ask? It seems like there's no checkmate, right? But white is not done and plays queen to F4 check. The third brilliant move in a row and the second queen sacrifice in the span of just three moves. And this puts the black king in a tough spot having to decide between checkmate or taking the seemingly free queen. But now white with only one pawn left against 26 points of material plays g5 checkmate and wins this game.
